'''Everett Lowell Kelly''' (November 15, 1905 – January 19, 1986) was an American clinical psychologist, professor of psychology at the [[University of Michigan]], president of the [[American Psychological Association]] (1954–55), and chairman of the Executive Committee for the [[Boulder Conference|Boulder Conference on Graduate Training in Clinical Psychology]] (1948–49).

== Biography ==
Kelly was born on November 15, 1905, in [[Kokomo, Indiana]].<ref name="NYT" /> He earned his Bachelor of Science degree at [[Purdue University]] in 1926, and his Master of Arts degree from [[Colorado College of Education]] two years later.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url = http://quod.lib.umich.edu/b/bhlead/umich-bhl-88402?view=text|title = BHL: Everett L. Kelly Papers 1926–1986|website = quod.lib.umich.edu|access-date = 15 March 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160318072939/http://quod.lib.umich.edu/b/bhlead/umich-bhl-88402?view=text|archive-date = March 18, 2016|url-status = live|df = mdy-all}}</ref> In 1930, he earned his PhD in Psychology from [[Stanford University]].<ref name=":0" /> His advisor was [[Walter Richard Miles|Walter R. Miles]], and his thesis focused on producing artificial chromaesthesia by the technique of controlled response.<ref>{{Cite journal|last = Kelly|first = E. Lowell|date = January 1, 1930|title = An experimental attempt to produce artificial chromaesthesia by the technique of the conditioned response ...|df = mdy-all|oclc = 24448167}}</ref>

After graduating, Kelly worked as a high school principal in [[Taiban, New Mexico]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url = http://www.lib.umich.edu/faculty-history/faculty/e-lowell-kelly/classroom-profile|title = Classroom Profile: Faculty History Project|website = lib.umich.edu|access-date = 15 March 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160316171049/http://www.lib.umich.edu/faculty-history/faculty/e-lowell-kelly/classroom-profile|archive-date = March 16, 2016|url-status = live|df = mdy-all}}</ref> Later, he became a member of the psychology faculty and director of admissions at the [[University of Hawaii]], followed by the [[University of Connecticut]].<ref name=":1" /> While at Hawaii, Kelly performed a psychological examination for the wife of Lieutenant Thomas S. Massie, which played a notable role in the famous [[Massie Trial]].<ref name="NYT">{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/1986/01/24/obituaries/dr-lowell-kelly-80-psychology-professor.html|title = Dr. Lowell Kelly, 80, psychology professor|date = January 24, 1986|work = [[The New York Times]]|access-date = November 12, 2014|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141112203512/http://www.nytimes.com/1986/01/24/obituaries/dr-lowell-kelly-80-psychology-professor.html|archive-date = November 12, 2014|url-status = live|df = mdy-all}}</ref>

From 1939 to 1942, Kelly worked as a member of the faculty and Director of the Psychological Clinic at [[Purdue University]].<ref name=":1" /> During [[World War II]], Kelly enlisted in the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]], where he worked on aviation medicine, aviation training, selection of pilots, and improvement of flight training methods.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=Autobiography of E. Lowell Kelly|last=Kelly|first=E. L.|publisher=A History of Psychology in Autobiography|year=1980|location=Akron, Ohio}}</ref> While in the Navy, Kelly was credited with discovering a common cause of military aviation crashes: cadets could not judge their distance from a plane with only one tail light. He introduced the notion of having two lights at a standard distance apart.<ref name="Fiske">{{cite journal|last2 = Conley|first2 = James|last3 = Goldberg|first3 = Lewis|year = 1987|title = E. Lowell Kelly (1905–1986)|journal = [[American Psychologist]]|volume = 42|issue = 5|pages = 511–512|doi = 10.1037/h0092035|last1 = Fiske|first1 = Donald}}</ref> For his contributions during the war, he was awarded the [[United States Secretary of the Navy|Secretary of Navy]]'s [[Commendation Medal|Letter of Commendation]].<ref name=":1" />

After the war, Kelly moved to the [[University of Michigan]], where he worked until his death in 1986.<ref name="Fiske" /> His scientific interests and contributions centered on assessment: job performance evaluations, psychological factors in marital compatibility, and assessment of qualifications for professional training.<ref name="Fiske" /> With [[Donald W. Fiske]], he published a classic study in 1950 on the prediction of performance of clinical psychologists.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url = http://psycnet.apa.org/psycinfo/1952-05949-000|title = The prediction of performance in clinical psychology.|website = APA PsycNET|access-date = 15 March 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160407000916/http://psycnet.apa.org/psycinfo/1952-05949-000|archive-date = April 7, 2016|url-status = live|df = mdy-all}}</ref> His other focus was [[Longitudinal study|longitudinal research]]. Overall, he studied such varied phenomena as [[synesthesia]], [[graphology]], [[pharmacology]], and [[Illusory motion|apparent movement]].<ref name="Fiske" />

Kelly served on the board of directors for the [[American Psychological Association|American Psychological Association (APA)]] for six years and was president of the Division of Consulting Psychology and the Division of Clinical Psychology.<ref name="Fiske" /> He was elected president of APA and served in that role from 1954 to 1955.<ref name="Fiske" /> He was also an adviser to the [[Selective Service System|National Selective Service]] and a consultant to agencies including the [[Veterans Administration]] (assessment of qualifications for professional training), the [[National Institutes of Health]], the [[Educational Testing Service]], the [[National Science Foundation]], and the [[United States Agency for International Development|Agency for International Development]].<ref name="NYT" /> Furthermore, he directed the selection division of the [[Peace Corps]].<ref name="NYT" />

Kelly died in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]], on January 19, 1986.<ref name="NYT" />

== Professional contributions ==

=== Performance assessment ===
Kelly conducted a number of studies assessing [[job performance]] and qualifications for professional training, with a particular emphasis on the field of [[clinical psychology]]. In his study of clinical psychology graduate students, Kelly evaluated numerous training programs from 40 different universities by a wide variety of techniques and made predictions concerning the students' probable success in training and their future job competence.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Mowrer|first=O. H.|date=January 1, 1953|title=Review of The Prediction of Performance in Clinical Psychology|jstor=1418750|journal=The American Journal of Psychology|volume=66|issue=2|pages=326–328|doi=10.2307/1418750|hdl=2027/mdp.39015014502648|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Furthermore, Kelly developed criterion measures of the several tasks which clinical psychologists are expected to perform in their training and later careers.<ref name=":4" /> In longitudinal studies, Kelly examined scholarly productivity, clinical performance, satisfaction, and attitudes about clinical psychology among students following their graduation and entrance into the workforce.<ref name=":4" /> Similar studies were conducted for other training programs, including programs for aircraft pilots in the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]]. As a part of that program, Kelly also developed a pilot aptitude test and a flight training manual with standardized vocabularies for naval [[flight instructor]]s.<ref name=":0" /> Kelly's research had a profound impact on the field of professional performance assessments, and several of his criterion measures and programs are continuously used in the field.<ref name=":4" />

=== Marital compatibility ===
One of Kelly's key areas of study was [[marital compatibility]], or identifying long-term patterns of marital adjustment that could be used as predictors of successful marriages in the future. His main findings were that personality adjustment, rather than social or cultural factors, were the basis for marital compatibility.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Kelly|first=E. Lowell|date=February 1, 1941|title=Marital Compatibility as Related to Personality Traits of Husbands and Wives as Rated by Self and Spouse|journal=The Journal of Social Psychology|volume=13|issue=1|pages=193–198|doi=10.1080/00224545.1941.9714069|issn=0022-4545}}</ref> In recent years, however, his research has fallen under scrutiny due to its emphasis on distinct [[gender role]]s and gender stereotypes that were universally endorsed at that time.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O5KLUxbqtT4C|title=Homeward Bound: American Families in the Cold War Era|last=May|first=Elaine Tyler|date=January 1, 2008|publisher=Basic Books|isbn=978-0786723461|language=en}}</ref> For instance, the questionnaires used asked women to assess their skills as "cooks" and "housemakers", while men were asked to rate themselves based on their capabilities as "providers" and "handymen".<ref name=":5" /> Furthermore, his published papers assessments focused almost exclusively on personal lives.<ref name=":5" /> Nevertheless, Kelly's data on this topic is still considered to be an important basis for the research on marital compatibility.<ref name=":6" />

=== Scientist-practitioner model ===
In 1948–49, Kelly chaired the Executive Committee for the [[Boulder Conference|Boulder Conference on Graduate Training in Clinical Psychology]].<ref name="Fiske" /> The purpose of the conference was to come up with a standard training plan for clinical psychologists. The result of the conference was the creation of the Boulder model, also known as the [[scientist-practitioner model]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1 = Baker|first1 = D. B.|last2 = Benjamin|first2 = L. T.|date = February 1, 2000|title = The affirmation of the scientist-practitioner. A look back at Boulder|journal = The American Psychologist|volume = 55|issue = 2|pages = 241–247|issn = 0003-066X|pmid = 10717972|doi=10.1037/0003-066x.55.2.241}}</ref> According to this model, clinical graduate students need to adhere to the scientific method in their applied practices. To do that, they need to complete monitored field work, receive research training, and attend seminars and lectures that strengthen their knowledge of psychology. This model argues that having sufficient knowledge and background in both research academia and applied practice enhances the psychologist's skills and abilities.<ref name=":2" />
